USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain the current posture and press the resumed talks without adding new commitments. We should use the already-imposed 25% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports, the standing threat of the ~$300B tranche, and Huawei's Entity List status as leverage to lock in a verifiable deal on purchases, enforcement, and structural IP/tech-transfer — not escalate, and not concede. Continue the constructive phone-level discussions (Liu He-Lighthizer-Mnuchin) toward a face-to-face round, and be willing to ease Huawei only against a concrete, matching Beijing commitment.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate (threat_score +0.35): the May escalation to 25% on List 3 plus the Huawei Entity List and Executive Order 13873 have already triggered real downside. The 10-year Treasury yield fell from ~2.74% (Jan) to ~2.06% (mid-July) and the 2-year from ~2.58% to ~1.83%, flattening/inverting key segments of the curve — a credible recession warning (web reporting notes the 3M-10Y segment inverted in May and flagged ~1.5% tariff drag pushing sub-2% growth toward recession risk). This is a genuine economic threat to US growth and the farm belt, which is why we cannot afford to escalate further. But the score stays moderate rather than existential because the US emerged from the G20 Osaka truce (Jun 29) holding the advantage: existing tariffs remain in place, the new $300B tranche is suspended 'for the time being', and China has agreed to resume talks and restart agricultural purchases, while Trump committed only to ease (not remove) Huawei restrictions. That leverage and favorable terrain keep this from the +0.5 anchor. The action stance (action_score +0.05, negotiate) reflects that this is the wrong moment for maximal escalation — imposing the $300B tariffs would break the truce, provoke full Chinese retaliation, deepen the yield-curve recession signal, and risk the 2020 domestic position — while a full concession would squander hard-won leverage. The disciplined move is to hold the tariff pressure and negotiate a firmer, enforceable deal, using Huawei relief as a quid pro quo rather than an upfront gift.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Enter the resumed talks in good faith and maintain the Osaka truce — do not escalate. Keep the negotiation channel open, signal continued willingness to purchase US agricultural goods as a confidence-building measure, but resist committing to structural reform of the state economy. Treat this pause as the window to secure relief on the existing ~$250B of 25% tariffs and to press for concrete, not merely rhetorical, easing of the Huawei entity-list restrictions, while deliberately avoiding any action that might reignite the $300B tariff threat.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but not existential at this point. Q2 GDP growth fell to 6.2%, its slowest since 1992 (China Daily/WaPo/NYT, July 15), and H1 exports fell 1.3% in dollar terms with exports to the US down 8.1% and imports from the US down 30% — clear evidence that the tariff regime (25% on ~$250B of goods, per timeline 2018-09-24 and 2019-05-10) is biting the export economy, and the entity-listing of Huawei (2019-05-16) is direct firm-level targeting of China's flagship tech champion. That supports a threat_score around the +0.5 anchor (major export sectors hit, firm-level targeting), tempered by the fact that growth remains within the government's 6%-6.5% band and stimulus is cushioning the blow. On the action side, escalation would be self-defeating: it risks collapsing the fragile truce and triggering the additional ~$300B of tariffs on the remaining Chinese exports that Washington explicitly held back at Osaka (2019-06-29; Reuters/Times). Because China's economy is already slowing, renewed escalation would deepen exactly the export and growth pain that drives the threat. Conversely, maximal concession is politically untenable given US demands run to structural changes in China's state-controlled economy (LA Times). The constructive middle is therefore to negotiate — keep the truce, build confidence through farm purchases, and work toward rolling back existing tariffs and clarifying Huawei relief — a mildly positive action stance consistent with a 'negotiate' posture and no new commitments.
